report.Subject: Interdisciplinary
report.Desc: The world's most populous country has a long, rich cultural tradition featuring unique views of life, persons, the human body, medicine, and nature. As China has sought to modernize over the last half century, some of its traditions and practices have persisted, while others have become Westernized. Part of a two-thousand-year-old tradition is the practice of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), which is still as vibrant today as in history. TCM, with its practice in acupuncture and herbal remedies, is becoming more and more recognized and popular in Western societies, including the US and Europe. With a holistic approach, TCM focuses more on improving the body’s natural ways of healing rather than combating diseases directly. Knowledge about and familiarity with TCM has increasing values for future healthcare professionals as well as for anyone interested in improving their own health. Half of this course focuses on Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), and the other half focuses on Chinese culture. Students will learn about Chinese history, philosophy, and culture in this class. China has a five-thousand-year-long recorded history with rich and distinctive cultures. As China becomes more and more influential on the global stage, an understanding of Chinese values and culture is increasingly important. When this course is offered off campus, students will learn TCM from a medical school in China and travel and explore various cities and cultural sites in China. When this course is offered on campus, students will learn from instructor(s) on campus and have field trips to Chinese restaurant, stores, churches, and Chicago Chinatown. In either case, students will experience Chinese culture firsthand. The course consists of lectures, discussions, presentations, an independent project, and trips.

report.Section_Title: The Impact of Clean Water: Kenya
report.Subject: Public Health
report.Desc: Rural communities in Honduras and Navajo Nation must rely on localized systems for clean water, usually point-of-use filtration. Students in this course will examine what types of interventions are sustainable and truly helpful. Students will learn how the availability of clean water relates to nutrition, poverty, life expectancy, education, employment, and income of the local community. Students will discern the nature of the problem regarding clean water availability on a local, national, and global level; and also wrestle with potential solutions to this pervasive and complex problem. Students will discuss the role of clean water in promoting equity, and access to clean water as a basic human right. Students will integrate various disciplines together to propose sustainable solutions that are culturally appropriate and charitably nontoxic. All enrolled students should plan on traveling over spring break to either Honduras or Navajo Nation. Travel costs will be paid for through a grant for the Clean Water Institute of Calvin University.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: This course is designed to guide class members through the issues and research literature related to communication within and from organizations and small groups. We focus on approaches, theories, and research findings concerning conceptions of organizations, various traditions in the study of organizations, metaphors for organizational communication, culture and climate within organizations, group processes, leadership, socialization/assimilation/membership negotiation, power, motivation/performance, organizational innovation and change, team-based structures and alternative forms of organizing, and strategic organizational communication. The unit of analysis undergirding the course is the actions of individuals or groups within organizations, especially actors’ messages and symbolic interactions, as well as the behavior of entire organizations or sets of organizations. Although organizations are such an ever-present, taken-for-granted aspect of our lives, you may not have developed a full understanding of them. For this reason, this course includes activities and assignments designed to enhance appreciation and analysis of organizations and organizational communication. The course also addresses competencies needed to communicate effectively in organizations and those skills useful for aiding others in organizations to attain personal and organizational goals.

report.Section_Title: The Impact of Clean Water: Honduras
report.Subject: Public Health
report.Desc: Rural communities in Honduras and Navajo Nation must rely on localized systems for clean water, usually point-of-use filtration. Students in this course will examine what types of interventions are sustainable and truly helpful. Students will learn how the availability of clean water relates to nutrition, poverty, life expectancy, education, employment, and income of the local community. Students will discern the nature of the problem regarding clean water availability on a local, national, and global level; and also wrestle with potential solutions to this pervasive and complex problem. Students will discuss the role of clean water in promoting equity, and access to clean water as a basic human right. Students will integrate various disciplines together to propose sustainable solutions that are culturally appropriate and charitably nontoxic. All enrolled students should plan on traveling over spring break to either Honduras or Navajo Nation. Travel costs will be paid for through a grant for the Clean Water Institute of Calvin University.

report.Desc: This course analyzes the social meanings of our various identities (i.e., race-ethnicity, class, and gender), how these identities affect our self-concepts, and the impact of these identities upon our social and societal relationships. report.Subject: Ministry Leadership (Handlon)
report.Desc: This course will explore restorative justice and the ideas that form its foundation, question its strengths and shortcomings, examine restorative practices , and investigate opportunities to put the theory into practice. Moreover, we will finetune our exploration of restorative justice from a religious point of view, and more specifically from a Christian point of view. We will note that several world religions provide a vision of what we are calling "restorative justice," and that Christianity puts a fine point on restorative justice as a form of "reconciliation." We will further explore how the church models a type of "commmunity of reconciliation" and as a model can inform how we might want to shape other social spaces into communities of restorative justice and reconciliation. For sections taught for the Calvin Prison Initiative, the social space we will consider is the Richard Handlon Correctional Facility. To that end, we will briefly take up issues of crime and punishment in the United States and relocate them in the realm of restorative justice and communities of reconciliation. report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: This course guides students in an examination of the social context of schooling, including the interaction and impact of social structures and systems on the educational experiences of individuals and groups. Particular attention is given to the study of race, class, and gender and how social science helps us understand their impact on schools, society, and learners. A biblically-guided understanding of justice helps shape this critical analysis. This course includes a 12-hour service-learning project centered on schools, communities, and families.

report.Section_Title: Curriculum, Instruction, and Content Area Literacy
report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: Students will develop an increased understanding of the complex issues surrounding learning theory and its impact on instruction in diverse educational contexts. Students will explore how an understanding of the learner, the curriculum, and the context shape instructional practice. They will learn how to engage in a pedagogical cycle that includes planning, implementation, evaluation, and reflection with a focus on meeting the needs of all learners. Students will also examine the nature and function of literacy in the secondary content curriculum. Specifically, this course will examine the reading and writing skills and practices that support the ways of knowing and doing characteristic of secondary school subject areas. All of these areas will be examined through the lens of a reformed Christian perspective. An extensive practicum will assist students in linking theory and practice in a classroom setting.

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: This internship provides field-based learning through a part-time placement in a grade 5-12 classroom. With the supervision of a faculty member and a master teacher, interns develop their understanding and performance of the knowledge, skills and dispositions expected of 5th- to 12th-grade educators. Individual observations, mentoring, and coursework aide interns in developing as professionals. Varied frameworks and tools are used throughout the internship to assess readiness for the professional field. A grade of C or higher along with the recommendation of the course instructor are required to continue in the education program.

report.Subject: Ministry Leadership
report.Desc: This course explores the beauty of the worldwide body of Christ, develops conceptual tools for learning to appreciate cultural differences in worship practices, and prepares students to participate in worship in different cultures as well as to talk with others from different cultures in gracious, hospitable, and discerning ways. Course activities include reading, discussion forums, viewing and (when applicable) participating in selected events such as the Calvin Symposium on Worship, and reflecting on the learning. Students are expected to attend university chapel services regularly throughout the course.

report.Subject: Finance
report.Desc: This course covers special topics in finance that will allow students more advanced study in specific areas of interest. Topics can include mergers and acquisitions, derivatives, capital markets, pensions, insurance, corporate valuation, credit analysis, real estate, capital budgeting, international finance, structured products, private investing, risk management, corporate social responsibility, financial planning, estate planning, retirement planning, and insurance planning and employee benefits. The topics may differ from year to year; if so, the course can be taken more than once.

report.Subject: Finance
report.Desc: This course requires students to synthesize and apply elements of comprehensive financial planning within a Christian context. The course requires students to perform all functions of the financial planning process and apply the CFP Board’s Practice Standards, including the development and delivery of a comprehensive financial plan. Additionally, this course will satisfy the educational requirements for the Certified Kingdom Advisor, CKA® designation (CKA). The course will contain two distinct elements: (1) online learning of approximately 15 modules related to the broad elements of the financial planning process; and (2) completion of a written comprehensive written financial plan for a “live” client and oral delivery of such plan. Students will utilize financial planning software in the preparation of the financial plan.

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: This course provides an exploration of the major approaches to development of a curriculum for infants, toddlers, and preschool-age children (birth to age six), the underlying assumptions of each approach, and the appropriateness of each approach for children. Special attention is given to supporting the development of early literacy and numeracy. This course includes a 6-hour per week field placement during the PK-12 school day.

report.Subject: Education

The course will focus on what it means to live out Christian faith commitments and practices in a variety of settings. This includes consideration of who teaches and is taught, what is taught, how and in what context we teach, and the complex ways in which these ideas interact and compete in a PK-12 classroom.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: In this course, we will learn both how to “read” and create images that persuade others. We will study the strengths and weaknesses of both images and words; using that knowledge, we can better analyze and create messages that use both visual and written rhetoric. We also will examine the ethical responsibility of both viewers and creators of images so that we are truthful, respectful, and fair in our practices. Building on this knowledge, we will finish the course with students creating intentional, ethical persuasive messages adapted to a well-defined target audience.

The student is introduced to digital logic families and programmable logic devices, digital logic CAD tools, logic synthesis and hardware description languages (VHDL).

Computer techniques will be frequently employed.

report.Subject: Engineering

This course exposes students to engineering approaches to analyzing and designing engineering solutions to sustainability challenges. Topics include sustainable energy systems, sustainability analysis methods, and collective action for sustainability. The biblical basis for sustainable living is explored.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: What is one of the top skills all employers look for in future employees? Effective oral communication. Being able to speak well in public also will help you in other courses, student and community groups, and in your church.  In this course you will learn the fundamental skills of oral rhetoric—how to create a message strategically adapted for a specific audience (for this semester, your fellow students in this class) and situation. You will also learn how to effectively deliver your speeches and how to be an engaged, thoughtful listener.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: Students will learn about their ethical responsibilities as professional communicators. They will investigate the principles on which those obligations and responsibilities are based—including social and cultural values, Christian virtues, and professional standards. In addition, they will learn to exercise moral and ethical reasoning when confronted with challenging situations in their vocation.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: An introduction to the principles and practice of communicating a message to an audience through digital images (still pictures, moving pictures, and graphics) and digital sound (voice, music, ambient sound, and sound effects). Students will learn the fundamental techniques of preproduction planning, camera use, lighting, sound, and editing in order to communicate their ideas effectively, artistically, and ethically. Students also will learn to communicate their messages through digital channels, especially the Internet. The course will enable students interested in social media, public relations, advertising, journalism, corporate training, sales, e-learning, publishing, worship, and the arts to realize ideas through sound and image. Students intending to take advanced Media Production courses must take COMM 190.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Locations: DeVos Communication Center 030A - Audio/Control Classroom; DeVos Communication Center 045 - Audio Corridor
report.Desc: This course introduces basic audio principles for filmmaking and podcasting, including interview and field recording techniques, and basic mixing, editing, and effects. This course is a prerequisite for COMM 290.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: This course introduces students to multitrack studio recording and front-of-house mixing techniques, including the use of advanced consoles and microphone setups.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: In this course students will examine how and why organizations use Advertising as a discipline to build and promote brands. The course emphasizes the professional tools and strategies used in the industry to employ best practices in effective and ethical mass communication.

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: This course will examine how Christian thinking about interdependent community can inform pedagogical designs and processes with a focus on the relational fabric constructed during learning and in the practices of schools. Students will examine biblical, confessional, theological, and educational sources on the nature of community and explore connections to educational practices before engaging in their own design process with explicit attention to its enactment of relational patterns.

report.Section_Title: Literacy Learning After the Early Years: Middle School Children, Adolescents and Adults
report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: This course supports educator's literacy development of middle school students, adolescents and adult literacy learners. Instructional emphases shift from the earlier years. Older literacy learners engage wide-ranging text forms and specialized vocabulary needs. Their school learning and work lives depend on abilities to interact purposefully and knowledgeably with print, digital or electronic texts. Increasingly self-directed, older learners need reading abilities to select apt comprehension strategies; respond critically to a reading; determine the applications of a text to other experience or situations; as well as determine objectives in their production of texts. Course participants: classroom teachers, coaches, resource room educators, community programmers, and adult literacy instructors, develop their professional knowledge and pedagogies to assist viewers and readers become more critical and discriminating readers and producers of texts.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: The intensive study and production of video in a particular style or genre. Thorough investigation of creative, ethical, and technical requirements will culminate in student productions of short films. Offered as fiction every spring semester, and as documentary in alternate fall semesters.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: An introduction to the theory and practice of communication and conflict resolution. Students will investigate the dynamics of conflict, theories of communication relevant to conflict resolution, conflict resolution processes and strategies. Students will learn skills that will enable them to assume leadership roles in the resolution of conflict, whether in the workplace, in the church, in political forums or at the international level. This knowledge can be applied in a variety of contexts: friendships, small groups, families, church, workplace, and community.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: Through careful study and practice of informal logic and rhetoric, students will become effective advocates, opponents, and decision makers in any argument context. The course is a study and application of basic principles of argumentation and advocacy. This course focuses on the dynamics of oral argument-ethical dimensions, use of language, informal logic, use of evidence and appeals, structure, and interactions with other arguments. Through analysis and practice, students will learn not only how to argue within academic contexts but also how to apply argumentative reasoning to everyday communication.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: An introduction to the practice and theory of directing. Through readings, critical analysis of scripts, discussions, performance exercises, and critique of live and filmed performance, students develop an understanding of the directing process from the inception of the script to the final product. Students create a full directorial analysis of a script and produce several finished scenes, applying rehearsal techniques, working with actors and learning to enhance their own productions through careful criticism and thoughtful assessment of the art of directing.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: An introduction to reporting for news media, using Associated Press guidelines, to write for digital and print publications. This course focuses on methods of news gathering, interviewing, and research with particular emphasis on reporting about current affairs. Students analyze trends and discuss ethical issues in contemporary journalism across a variety of platforms, but their primary focus is on the writing and editing of news.

report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: A study of the role of diverse forms of media in society and an examination of critical and cultural perspectives on media. The course examines the media as a source of influential narratives and offers an understanding of the relationship of media to democracy, capitalism, technology, audiences, media institutions, and economics.

report.Section_Title: Special Topics: Post Color and Sound
report.Subject: Communication
report.Locations: DeVos Communication Center 065 - Video Control Classroom
report.Desc: Topic, readings, and assignments will be announced prior to the year offered. Designed for students from various majors.
report.Notes: Special Topic: Post Color and Sound: This course offers an intensive, half-semester exploration of advanced post-production practices for film and media production. Emphasis is placed on professional color-grading workflows, including color correction, creative grading, and delivery for different viewing contexts. Students will also engage selective topics in audio post-production. Through hands-on projects and applied exercises, students develop technical proficiency and critical judgment appropriate for upper-level media production work.

report.Section_Title: Advanced Comm Study: Global Film and Media
report.Subject: Communication
report.Desc: A focused study of selected topics in a discipline of communication (film, media, or rhetoric) that builds upon previous communication coursework, methods, and theories. Coursework involves lecture, discussion, seminar presentations, and the preparation of a major research paper or project.
report.Notes: Special topic description: This course explores the role of film and media in a global society. Through critical analysis of film, television, and digital platforms, students will examine how popular media reflect and are shaped by social, historical, political, and economic forces that often transcend national borders. Topics include transnational and national cinemas, media and migration, globalization and media flows, and the influence of new technologies on the global production, distribution, and reception of media.

report.Subject: English
report.Desc: Writing Studio offers students extra support in academic writing in a small group tutoring context. The focus of instruction is the students' own writing from other courses. Instructors and tutors help students understand writing assignments--reflect upon specific guidelines, goals, and contexts--and provide support through the drafting, revision, and editing phases. Course may be repeated up to three times for elective credit; graded credit/no credit.

report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: Students will integrate academic learning into social work practice through the completion of a 400-hour social work field education experience paired with a weekly professional seminar. The professional seminar will allow students to process their field experiences. Students will apply areas of social work content to experiences in the field, including professionalism, the planned change process, social policy, human diversity, and professional ethics. Within the field setting, students will interact with client systems at the individual, family, group, community, and organizational levels, and will process these interactions with their peers in the professional seminar. Prerequisite: admission to the BSW program and field education.

report.Subject: Computer Science
report.Desc: Design principles and implementation issues of contemporary programming languages. Topics covered include programming paradigms; the syntax and semantics of programming language constructs, including those that support concurrent, parallel, and distributed processing; translation of high-level languages to machine language; formal languages and the automata that recognize them. Several different languages are introduced and examined to illustrate these topics. Lab fee - see catalog for details.

Topics covered include programming paradigms; the syntax and semantics of programming language constructs, including those that support concurrent, parallel, and distributed processing; translation of high-level languages to machine language; formal languages and the automata that recognize them. Several different languages are introduced and examined to illustrate these topics. Lab fee - see catalog for details.

report.Subject: Computer Science
report.Desc: This seminar explores a range of current topics in computing, including topics in research and practice. It is a continuation of CS 195. Department majors must take this course three times during their junior and senior years.

report.Subject: Computer Science
report.Desc: This course provides a holistic introduction to the support of organizational information technology cloud computing and services. It covers cloud computing platforms, services, and their use in business information technology administration. Students work with open source and commercial platforms. Students apply these skills through multiple system implementation labs and team projects.

report.Subject: Science Education Studies
report.Locations: Science Building 255 - Elementary Educ Science Class
report.Desc: This course targets scientific and engineering practices and skills foundational to scientific and engineering literacy. Content covered includes the role of models in science, forces and the particulate nature of matter, scientific testing, and engineering practices. Special attention is given to developing a theological understanding of how God works in nature and how creation manifests God's grandeur.

report.Subject: Studio Art
report.Desc: Equipped with a basic typographic proficiency, students in this course will hone their technical and conceptual skills through close examination of the structural elements of design. Hierarchy, grid systems, and organizational strategies are central concerns. Complex communication problems are addressed, incorporating formal and expressive typography, pictorial imagery, and personal narratives. Conceptually, distinctions between the analysis of form and the meanings of form are explored. Assignments range from the production of a multi-page publication using InDesign to the development of a design project using found materials.

report.Subject: Speech Pathology & Audiology
report.Desc: This course provides a supervised clinical experience in which the student clinician observes individuals who have various speech, language, or hearing impairments under the supervision of a speech-language pathologist or audiologist. This course is required as the initial field experience for speech pathology and audiology majors and is designed to introduce students to general therapy and assessment procedures across the disciplines.

report.Subject: Engineering
report.Desc: An intermediate treatment of heat transfer and thermodynamics including analysis and design related to steady and unsteady conduction with an emphasis on two and three dimensions, free and forced convection, radiation modes of heat transfer, power and refrigeration cycles, air conditioning processes, chemical equilibrium, and combustion. Laboratory, design, and computer exercises are utilized to emphasize principles.

report.Subject: Engineering
report.Desc: Feedback principles and electronic circuit theory and device theory applied to multistage transistor amplifiers. Detailed study of operational amplifier specs, non-idealities, and compensation. Introduction to filter theory and practical realizations. Power supply design: Rectifier circuits, linear, and switching regulators. Nonlinear circuits: Comparators, multipliers, Schmitt trigger, S/H circuits, multi-vibrators, and oscillators. Introduction to noise analysis and low noise design. Emphasis on realization of designs using commercially available ICs. Design experience emphasized in projects.

report.Section_Title: Dynamics of Machinery and Instrumentation Lab
report.Subject: Engineering
report.Desc: This laboratory serves as an introduction to the characteristics and uses of transducers to measure displacement, strain, pressure, temperature, velocity, acceleration, and other physical quantities. Emphasis is on the usefulness, accuracy, and reliability of measurement systems in actual applications. Electronic signal conditioning techniques are covered. A design project using LabVIEW software and data acquisition hardware is required. Written reports required.

The course will include attention to how the Bible, with its diversity of genres, functions as an educational text, as well as to exemplars of Christian engagement with education and key facets of teacher and student vocation. A range of faith-informed practices will be examined as they apply to professional practice in educational settings.

A range of faith-informed practices will be examined as they apply to professional practice in educational settings.

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: In this course students consider how to teach the social studies through inquiry, with a special emphasis on children PreK through grade 6. Knowledge development will focus primarily on the geographic, sociocultural and global threads of the social studies. The inquiry process will be modeled with an exploration of a global region. Participants will develop their skills in core teaching practices.

report.Section_Title: Introduction to Cognitive Impairment: Birth through School Age
report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: A comprehensive study of the characteristics of infants and children who have cognitive impairment, intellectual or developmental disability, or developmental delay. Common causes, medical and school-based definitional issues, assessment, eligibility for special education, and interventions will be discussed. While special attention is given to supports for children with cognitive impairment as learners, the course examines functioning across a variety of settings besides the school, such as the church, home, and neighborhood. A Christian view of persons, community, and discipleship, along with the concepts of inclusion, social role valorization, and self-determination are integrating elements in the course. Seven hours of observation in a local school or early childhood program is required for this course.

report.Section_Title: Introduction to Cognitive Impairment: Transition to Adulthood
report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: A comprehensive study of the characteristics of persons who have intellectual disability. Historical and contemporary perspectives on intellectual disability will be explored, as will common causes, definitional issues, and interventions. The course examines the transition to adulthood in a variety of settings besides the school, such as the church, workplace, and neighborhood. A Christian view of persons, community, and discipleship, along with the concepts of normalization, social role valorization, and self-determination are integrating elements in the course. Seven hours of observation in a transition or adult services program is required for this course.

report.Section_Title: Teaching Social Studies in Elementary Grades
report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: Students consider social studies content and pedagogy for children from PreK through grade 6. Knowledge development will focus primarily on the political and economic threads of the social studies. The inquiry process and other social studies instructional strategies will be further developed with an emphasis on finding quality sources (including children’s and adolescent literature) for children’s exploration of social studies content and issues in the social studies. Participants develop and demonstrate core teaching practices during peer teaching and practicum experiences.

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: Taking an interdisciplinary perspective, students will consider the question, “What contributes to flourishing in learning communities?,” particularly when faced with a contemporary challenge. Pulling from experiences in their full-time internship in a P-12 classroom, previous program coursework, research, and personal inquiries, students will select a challenge that transpires in their assigned placement. They will consider how self, context and the core aspects of teaching (pedagogy, curriculum, assessment, and classroom management) along with a Reformed Christian worldview inform their response and engage practice in ways that foster greater flourishing for all.

report.Subject: Music
report.Locations: Covenant Fine Arts Center 115 - Swets Choral Hall; Covenant Fine Arts Center - Recital Hall
report.Desc: Study and performance of choral literature related to the practice of Christian worship throughout the history of the church and in many cultures. Emphasis on vocal and musical development, as well as on the theological, historical, and liturgical dimensions of selected choral repertoire. Open to all students who meet the requirements of voice and musicianship.

report.Subject: Music
report.Locations: Covenant Fine Arts Center 125 - Multipurpose Rm
report.Desc: Study and performance of music for small ensembles. Instrumentalists, pianists, and singers may take this course. Students are expected to participate in the selection of music to be studied and to assume leadership in organizing ensembles, rehearsing, and performing, with guidance and support provided by music faculty. Membership is open to all students who meet the demands of musicianship.

report.Subject: Music
report.Desc: A public performance of a minimum of 50 minutes of music. Fee (only for recitals not required by degree program) - see catalog for details.

report.Subject: Music
report.Desc: A public performance of a minimum of 25 minutes of music. Fee (only for recitals not required by degree program) - see catalog for details. Prerequisites: four semesters of MUSC 260 - Private Lessons for Credit and permission of your private-lesson instructor and area supervisor.

report.Subject: Marketing
report.Desc: A study of the principles and strategies for planning and controlling marketing programs, including the market research, product development, pricing, promotion, and distribution of ideas, goods, services, experiences, and values that attempts to satisfy individual and organizational needs and objectives. Includes real-world learning projects.

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: The purpose of this course is to provide students with the opportunity to deepen their understanding of their chosen area of study and to specialize their focus through an extended program of reading guided by an instructor. Students will negotiate with their instructor a program of 2000 pages of reading (or equivalent) in their chosen area and evidence engagement with this literature through written and oral reports.

report.Section_Title: Teaching Science in Elementary and Middle Grades: Internship I
report.Subject: Science Education Studies
report.Locations: Off Campus; Science Building 276 - General Biology
report.Desc: A consideration of the methods, pedagogies, and strategies associated with teaching science in grades K-9. Curricular resources for teaching science, including the use of technology and written materials, are also examined with consideration of the criteria for their evaluation. Additional topics include assessment, benchmarks and standards, and lesson and unit development. The relationship of Christian faith to the teaching of science in the classroom is also examined. Field experiences during normal course hours are included.

report.Subject: Science Education Studies
report.Desc: A consideration of the methods, pedagogies, and strategies associated with teaching science in middle school. Curricular resources for teaching science, including the use of technology and written materials, are also examined with consideration of the criteria for their evaluation. Additional topics include assessment, benchmarks and standards, and lesson and unit development. The relationship of Christian faith to the teaching of science in the classroom is also examined. Field experiences during normal course hours are included.

report.Section_Title: Framing Questions, Global Forces, Constraining Structures
report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: This course will center on fundamental questions at the intersection of education, justice, and human flourishing. We will examine key issues surrounding the nature of a good society, the ways in which the global community affects education, and how schooling gets structured by politics and economics. This course will use the faith-based frames of justice and hope in connection with shalom and the kingdom of God to investigate formal education in light of its political, economic, social, and religious contexts. Students will investigate foundational questions around teaching, learning, curriculum, and language as well as structural issues of social class, gender, ability, and race. The aim is for students to articulate their own idea of the purpose of school framed in their own faith-based perspective. The course will leave space for students to explore specific interests and issues.

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: This course engages students in understanding and examining the theories, methods, and paradigmatic frames of educational research through a biblical lens. In addition, the course prepares students to use data appropriately to support educational and organizational decision-making. Students will learn how to read and critique qualitative and quantitative educational research and will learn how to use research and assessment data to make decisions related to the work of P-12 schools.

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: Students examine education in its context as a life practice. It involves inquiry into and critique of the philosophical assumptions, historical developments, and social settings that shape the beliefs and practices informing schools as social institutions and education as a cultural practice. Throughout the course, students are developing their own faith-based philosophy of education.  Prerequisites: Junior or senior standing, EDUC 240, and Internship I (EDUC 308; or EDUC 315, EDUC 350, MATH 324 and SCES 310).

report.Subject: Education
report.Desc: This internship provides field-based learning through a full-time placement in a grade K-12 classroom. With the supervision of faculty members and master teachers, candidates refine their understanding and performance of the knowledge, skills and dispositions expected of educators. Individual observations, mentoring, and coursework aid candidates in developing as professionals. Varied frameworks and tools are used throughout the internship to assess readiness for the professional field. Students will complete a project tailored to their disciplinary pedagogy interests.

report.Subject: Education
report.Notes: Independent study of topics of interest to particular students under supervision of a member of the department staff. The requirements for credit are determined by the supervising faculty member in collaboration with the student. Open to qualified students with permission of the Master of Education program director.

report.Subject: Economics
report.Desc: An introduction to economics in the context of a study of health economics and health policy, with detailed focus on the US health care system. The intent of the course is to develop an understanding of economic principles that can be used with other criteria to evaluate the historical and future direction of the US health care system. Topics include efficiency and equity of resource allocation, ethical perspectives on health care access, history and current direction of US and international health care policy, and the development and evolution of insurance, hospital and health care provider markets. This course is recommended for students seeking a professional career in health care management, human resources, medicine, mental health professions, nursing, public health or public policy.

report.Subject: Economics
report.Desc: An intermediate-level study of macroeconomic theory emphasizing modeling and analysis of general business activity and the implications of changing business conditions for business planning and public policy. Computer lab work is used to understand the implications of economic policy.

report.Subject: Economics
report.Desc: This course provides a deeper, more comprehensive understanding of economic thought and/or microeconomic and macroeconomic theories and applications. Topics vary.

report.Subject: Economics
report.Desc: This course investigates how people and firms in market economies make economic decisions. Students will explore the environmental and societal implications of economic growth, unemployment, and inflation. Furthermore, Christian views concerning justice, freedom, stewardship, and the nature of human beings and society are applied to economic analysis and issues.

report.Subject: Engineering
report.Desc: This course involves study of selected special topics of current interest in engineering. Topics vary by year and may be focused on interdisciplinary problem-solving or design, advanced theoretical or experimental analysis, and/or explorations of disciplinary breadth. Consult the department website for specific sections and topics that will be offered. This course may be repeated for credit if the title and associated content differs.

report.Subject: Engineering
report.Desc: An introduction to load estimation, failure criteria, and design techniques for aircraft wing and fuselage sections. Wing section properties are discussed using beam-column moments, torsion of thin-walled and skin-stringer multiple-cell sections, flexural shear, cut-outs and shear lag, modified beam theory for design, and the fundamentals of static aeroelasticity. Properties of fuselage sections are reviewed including modified beam theory, linear elastic plate theory, linear elastic shell theory, numerical techniques for complex structures, and failure modes of plates and shells.

report.Subject: Engineering
report.Desc: Engineering students who complete engineering-related internship or research work may receive transcript credit for the experience. Completion of the internship course requires a minimum of 140 hours of experiential learning, consisting of engineering professional work or academic research that emphasizes application of the knowledge and skills gained in engineering coursework. Internship projects must be guided by engineering practitioners and will be evaluated by the engineering department internship coordinator. Students must submit an internship plan, reflect on the internship experience, submit a brief written report of their activities under the signature of their supervisor, and summarize their work in a poster presentation. Questions regarding the appropriateness of specific experiential learning activities for internship credit should be directed to the engineering internship coordinator.

report.Desc: Sustainability seeks to serve the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This course examines the challenges to that goal in each of the three areas of sustainability: economic, societal, and environmental. Topics include the biblical basis for sustainability, global energy consumption and carbon emissions, application areas for sustainability, and personal and collective actions.

report.Subject: Interdisciplinary
report.Desc: Sustainability Experience involves a minimum of 100 hours per semester (or equivalent) in a professional setting with an approved sustainability-themed project in a research, business, or nonprofit organization. Academic work includes class meetings and in-person and online discussions, an assessment from the employer-supervisor, readings, seminars/workshops, reflective journals, and participation in the sustainability showcase. Primarily for students pursuing the sustainability designation.

report.Desc: Students will explore practices for maintaining their own physical and mental health, including daily health maintenance; avoiding health problems; improving exercise, sleep, eating, and stress management habits; accessing medical help; and utilizing health insurance. They will identify and practice safe self-administration of medication and maintain a safety plan for avoiding health hazards. Students will discuss the importance of making healthy decisions regarding sexual relationships. Furthermore, they will identify the signs of emotional, sexual, and physical abuse and identify strategies, information, resources, and steps needed to end abuse.

They will compile their completed research; determine the best methods to communicate the information in formal and informal settings; design and create their own research presentation; and share it with peers, professors, and community members at a research fair on campus.

report.Desc: This course addresses social, ethical, legal and professional issues that arise in computer science from a reformed, Christian perspective. Ethical discussion starts with a survey of ethical theories and covers professional, ethical and legal issues in areas including intellectual property, privacy, liability and professional codes of conduct. In addition, some foundational issues are covered, including materialist vs. Christian view of what it means to be a person.

Topics such as computer-aided manufacturing (CAM), numerical control (NC), statistical quality control (SQC), and quality management are also explored. Field trips and laboratories are used to support the lecture material.

The course focuses on basic nerve cell function, neuroanatomy, and how lower level brain systems function in our everyday behavior. Specific topics include the relationship of brain function to basic visual and other sensory processes (e.g., hearing, touch, and pain), sleep, sexuality, basic motivations such as hunger and thirst, basic emotional functions, and basic memory and learning processes. Teacher candidates in this course will reflect upon the relationship between one’s faith/worldview and teaching of mathematics. The course is taken concurrently with field placements in grades PK-3 and/or 3-6. Corequisites: EDUC 315, EDUC 530 and SCES 310.

Topics include descriptive statistics, probability theory, random variables and probability distributions, sampling distributions, point and interval estimation, hypothesis testing, analysis of variance, and correlation and regression. Students may not receive credit for both STAT 143 and STAT 145.

Topics include: 1) the physical nature of Earth’s surface based on materials (rocks and minerals), plate tectonics, and the processes that create landforms; 2) the roles and movements of water in the atmosphere, oceans, surface water, and groundwater; and 3) weather components, storms, and climate systems. Understanding of Earth systems is applied to concepts of stewardship and human interactions with Earth’s environments. Not open to students who have completed GEO 151 or 153.

Theoretical frameworks and models help students understand patterns of migration, settlement, land use, agriculture, industry, religion, language, ethnicity, and territorial control.

report.Section_Title: Senior Seminar in Geology, Geography, and Environment
report.Subject: Geology & Geography
report.Desc: In this course, students in geology, geography, environmental studies and environmental science programs are guided through an exploration of the history, philosophy, and contemporary issues of their own discipline. Common themes of developing a Christian philosophy, understanding the history of a discipline, the nature of inquiry and understanding, and human-environment relationships provide structure to the course. Students are grouped by majors in breakout sessions where discussion reaches deeper into disciplinary knowledge. Students will lead sessions for the whole class on interesting issues, problems or controversies within their discipline. The course format encourages each student to think deeply about their own discipline and build mutual communication with students in related disciplines.

report.Subject: Chemistry

Topics covered include periodicity, bonding, symmetry, and reactivity. Special attention will be given to visualization tools for molecular structures. Upon completion of the course, students will be prepared to critically compare and contrast molecular and biomolecular structures with chemical reactions presented in subsequent course work throughout the science division.

report.Subject: Chemistry
report.Desc: Fundamental analytical and synthetic techniques associated with an inorganic chemistry laboratory will be learned. This includes the ability to safely run aqueous inorganic reactions and characterize products using a wide array of techniques (UV-Visible Absorbance, Magnetometry, Cyclic voltammetry, and Computational Chemistry). A lab notebook will be maintained, and completed experiments will be summarized in written lab reports.

report.Subject: Chemistry
report.Desc: How do you create increasingly large and complex molecules? Central to answering this question is the ability to control a reaction’s mechanism, product distribution, or material properties. This course will focus on the synthesis of complicated molecules. Synthesis encompasses a variety of strategies, such as total synthesis, biosynthesis, and polymeric synthesis. Special attention will be paid to asymmetric control of traditional organic reactions, particularly using catalytic methods, as well as the growing application of catalysis and synthetic methods for the generation of high-performance polymers.

Finally, students learn how to “listen” to a map through a series of exercises on how to evaluate and understand maps. Crosslisted as GEO 560.

report.Subject: Geology & Geography
report.Desc: This course uses the principles and methods of geology to reconstruct the history of Earth. This course studies the vastness of geologic time and investigates changes in Earth, gradual and sudden, over this deep time. Preserved evidence of past geologic events and history of life is discussed; this includes interpreting fossil records and rock records to better understand events that took place in the past. Topics include the origin of Earth and its moon, the origin of continents and ocean basins, the creation of mountain ranges through history, the formation of major sedimentary deposits, and Earth's climate history.

report.Desc: This course reflects on the moral dimension of life as a whole, in its relation to what we believe, what we do, and what sorts of people we want to be. It studies basic ethical questions such as the objectivity of right and wrong, what justice is, how we ought to live, why we should try to be morally good. It considers these questions both theoretically and practically (by applying them to issues in contemporary social life, such as capital punishment or abortion). It also uses both historical sources (such as Aristotle and Kant) and contemporary sources. Finally, it considers what difference Christian faith makes to the theory and the practice of morality. There may be a service-learning component in the course, depending on the instructor.

report.Subject: Philosophy
report.Desc: While Enlightenment myths narrate modernity as an escape from faith, this course demonstrates that, in fact, the opposite is true: Christian questions, assumptions, and commitments propelled modern thought. The course examines the Christian intellectual foundations of modernity in key figures such as Descartes, Leibniz, Pascal, Kant, Kierkegaard, and Hegel (as well as their debates with figures like Hume and Nietzsche). Philosophical questions in modernity arose from existential struggles at the intersection of faith and reason including the haunting of doubt, the problem of evil, and the foundations for the good life. Emphasis is placed on the practice of philosophy--e.g., dialogue, charitable interpretation of texts, clear argumentation in writing--and on historically and contextually-sensitive faith-based engagement with philosophical ideas as an ongoing part of a reflective Christian life.

Prerequisite: two or more philosophy courses, or one philosophy course plus junior or senior standing.

In addition, the course introduces common enterprise structures that support corporate information needs, including foundational concepts in information technology such as networking, relational databases, cloud resources, and data collection technologies (e.g., RFID, IoT). The course explores interorganizational systems like Electronic Data Interchange (EDI), blockchain, and related standards, while introducing students to ethical considerations in technology, emphasizing privacy, honesty, consent, and the concept of shalom in tech ethics. report.Subject: Recreation
report.Locations: Hoogenboom Health & Recreation 270 - Human Performance Lab
report.Desc: This course provides a general orientation to therapeutic recreation and its role in serving the needs of diverse diagnostic groups. The etiology, characteristics, and considerations for treatment of a wide range of common diseases and disorders are reviewed and discussed. Practical applications and adaptations for serving the functional and health needs of persons with disabilities will be made.

report.Section_Title: Introduction to Practice: Communities and Organizations
report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: Framed by change theory and the social work value of advocacy, this course will introduce students to understanding macrolevel social work with communities, organizations, and institutions. Faith-rooted community social work and congregational social work will also be explored.

report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: This course will provide an overview of the theories such as identity theory, person-in-environment theory, and family systems theory as a framework for engaging with adolescents and their families. Topics will include typical adolescent development, environmental influences, and common adolescent mental health disorders. Students will be introduced to engagement skills such as trust and rapport building and assessment skills such conducting mental status exams. The course will also review interventions such as mindfulness, internal family systems, and interpersonal therapy.

report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: The social work program evaluation course provides students with the knowledge and skills necessary to design, implement, and critically assess program evaluations within diverse social work settings. Emphasizing the vital role of evaluation in promoting accountability, effectiveness, and equity, the course prepares students to become reflective practitioners who use evidence to inform and improve service delivery. Students will engage with the purpose and types of program evaluation (formative, summative, process, and outcome), logic models and theory of change frameworks, data collection and analysis methods, ethical and culturally responsive evaluation practices, and strategies for engaging stakeholders and communicating findings. Students will engage in real-world case studies and apply a critical lens to evaluation effectiveness and efficiency of social programs.

report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: The MSW capstone course provides students an opportunity to integrate the content of their social work courses and a Christian worldview. This capstone course allows students to explore a specific social work issue with depth and application to their future career by incorporating each of the nine CSWE competencies and a faith perspective in a major project. Topics such as resiliency, self-sustainability, and licensure will also be explored.

report.Subject: Recreation
report.Desc: Experiential education is an essential component of a student's learning before entering the field of recreational therapy services as a professional practitioner. The design of the recreation internship provides majors with a full-time structured learning experience in a recreational therapy setting of the student's choice. The internship offers students an opportunity to bridge the gap between theory and practice as well as move from being a student to a professional. With this in mind, students are encouraged to take more of an active role in setting up their internship as well as customizing assignments and due dates to fit with the outcomes they are seeking by completing their internship. Prerequisite: Therapeutic Recreation majors must first complete all courses in the recreation program. All students must have a minimum cumulative grade point average of C (2.0) and the approval of the department advisor.

report.Subject: History
report.Desc: A survey of African-American history from West African societies to contemporary times. Highlights include the creation of a slave society in British North America, African-American intellectual traditions, the African-American church, and social and political movements for freedom, with a special emphasis on the substance and symbolism of the Obama years.

report.Subject: History
report.Desc: This is not a military history course. Instead, the course examines the social and cultural contexts of warfare from a global and comparative perspective. Case studies are drawn from different conflicts during the 20th century in different world regions, such as Austria-Hungarian World War I, Japan after World War II, post-colonial West Africa, and the recent wars of the United States. By examining the histories of individual states during particular conflicts, students will seek to understand why governments and societies move toward military action and how states, societies, and individuals are affected by war.

report.Subject: History
report.Desc: Wallace Stegner once said that the West is America, only more so. This is especially true of mythologies of the frontier West. They embody some of America’s most powerful national ideas, from rugged individualism to progressive and conservative forms of American exceptionalism. This course surveys the mythologies of the frontier West as found in scholarly and popular history writing, regional fiction, science fiction, Wild West shows, film, television, painting, photography, theme parks, and political campaigns. It compares American frontier mythologies to similar traditions in other “settler” societies. It explores what mythologies are, how they have shaped national identities, and how they can be used politically. It also examines them from the viewpoint of Biblical narratives and Christian worldview and theology.

report.Subject: Art History
report.Desc: What do people wear, and why? This course explores the past five centuries of fashion history with an eye toward understanding today's sartorial conventions. The course starts from a commitment to the simple proposition that clothing matters a lot. Attending to ethical questions of production as well as consumption, the course addresses five major themes: the mediation of the body, gender representations, style, modernist constructions of consumer culture, and performance.

report.Section_Title: History of the West and the World I
report.Subject: History
report.Desc: A survey of world history from the late Paleolithic to the beginnings of European overseas expansion (c. 1500 CE), highlighting the development of agrarian societies, the evolution of the world's major religious and cultural traditions, human migration and intercultural encounters, and impulses from these as seen in gender and class relations, technological exchange, and political and economic interchange and conflict.

Emphasis on vocal and musical development, as well as on the theological, historical, and liturgical dimensions of selected choral repertoire. report.Desc: An application of finance theory to investment instruments, including stocks, bonds, mutual funds, options, and futures, as well as the related investment theory including risk, return, valuation, and asset allocation. The course also examines the financial markets and institutions through which these instruments trade, including investment companies, funds, exchanges, and clearing houses. The course will challenge students to critically evaluate investment principles and practices from a Christian perspective. The primary perspective taken in the course is that of a finance professional (institutional), though we will also cover select topics from the perspective of personal investment decision-making and personal finance.

report.Subject: Supply Chain Management
report.Instructors: Rachel Hammond; Frederick Haan; Philip Johnson; Adrian Sanchez
report.Desc: The Global Supply Chain Practicum is an international travel course required for students pursuing the OSCM major. This course is offered during Winter Intensive of the spring term and will focus on the impact of operations and global supply chain decisions in the context of local flourishing and economic impact. This course involves engagement with key technical aspects of manufacturing and operations management but also allows students to engage with reflective readings and writing considering the impact of economic opportunity, development and ethical leadership primarily focused on economic deserts. SCM 311 is an off-campus course. Note: students must take both SCM 310 and SCM 311 in consecutive terms.

report.Subject: Ministry Leadership
report.Desc: Students learn to address specific situations, problems, challenges, and opportunities in ministry through interdisciplinary readings, theological reflection, and strategic planning exercises. Each section of CMS 251 focuses on a unique topic. Students are encouraged to enroll in the course up to 4 times.

report.Subject: Chemistry
report.Desc: This course is a study of the basic principles of chemistry, with emphasis on the laws of chemical combination; descriptive inorganic chemistry; thermochemistry; the gas, liquid, and solid states of matter; the periodic law; atomic structure; and chemical bonding. ...The course is taught from a biblical and reformed worldview and addresses issues such as the validity and limitations of scientific knowledge, the methodology of the physical sciences, human responsibility in applying such knowledge in society, and the care and stewardship of natural resources. Prerequisite: one year of high-school chemistry or permission of the instructor.

report.Subject: Chemistry

report.Section_Title: Human Behavior and the Social Environment
report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: This course involves studying persons in their environment with a focus on human behavior and development using a Reformed perspective of creation, fall, redemption. Persons are described as biological, psychological, social, cultural, and spiritual beings who grow and develop throughout their lives. Theoretical frameworks, with special emphasis on systems perspectives, are applied to enable students to explore and assess micro, mezzo, and macro influences on human behavior and development.

report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: This course critically explores how social welfare policies in the United States affect client systems. Students will examine how structural and institutional barriers influence social welfare policy and practices. Students are introduced to the history of social welfare policies that influence social work practice. Students will evaluate and analyze policies and develop practical advocacy skills in human rights and social, economic, and environmental justice.

report.Section_Title: Ethical Leadership and Social Work Supervision
report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: This course examines the challenges and importance of ethical leadership as it relates to stewarding authority, recognizing bias, character development, and increasing awareness regarding different cultural values. The course will also offer practical exploration of a supervisor's administrative, educational, and supportive roles and the task of evaluating others. The impact of secondary trauma, compassion fatigue and the importance of self care in leadership will also be reviewed.

report.Section_Title: Working with Infants, Children, and Families
report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: This course will provide an overview of the theories and social work practice for working with infants, children, and families. Topics will include child development theory, attachment theory, and family systems theory. The course will also review common childhood mental health disorders. Students will be introduced to engagement skills such as trust and rapport building and assessment skills such conducting mental health exams. The course will also introduce interventions such as emotion regulation strategies, play therapy, and family structural therapy.

report.Section_Title: Communities and Organizations II: Nonprofit Management
report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: This course will equip MSW students with the understanding of what it means to be a leader in the nonprofit sector. Through a critical lens grounded in social justice and systems theory, students will explore the unique challenges and opportunities inherent in nonprofit leadership, including governance, fundraising with government and philanthropic organizations, financial stewardship and managing a budget, program development, and community engagement. Emphasis is placed on the role of nonprofits in responding to complex social needs. In the course, students will work collectively to analyze organizational case studies and engage in strategic planning. Students will also have the opportunity to engage with practitioners to incorporate theory into practice. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to lead and foster sustainable change within communities and organizations.

report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: This praxis-oriented course is a continuation of SOWK 580. This course requires the completion of the 400-hour onsite practicum (spread over SOWK 580 and this course). The practicum will be accompanied by a synchronous online seminar. Guided by a biblical perspective and NASW values, students will apply areas of social work content to experiences in the practicum, including professionalism, the planned change process, social policy, anti-oppressive practice, and professional ethics. Within the practicum setting, students will engage, assess, and intervene and evaluate with client systems at the individual, family, group, community, and organizational levels.

report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: This praxis-oriented course continues the work started in SOWK 680 and provides continuation of on-site learning opportunity for students to demonstrate achievement of the nine CSWE competencies in a specialized social work practice setting. Students will complete a 500-hour internship in a social work setting where they will work toward mastery of generalist social work skills (engagement, assessment, intervention, evaluation, and termination) and those related to one's specialization. On-site practicum is accompanied by a weekly seminar where students connect with a faculty liaison and learn from peers' experiences. Licensure requirements as they relate to the nine competencies will also be reviewed.

report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: Students will learn about the generalist intervention model in social work practice with individuals, families and groups. They will develop practice competencies in solution-focused interviewing with individuals, examining family systems, and exploring group dynamics. Special attention will be to anti-racist and anti-oppressive practice and to competent and ethical documentation.

report.Subject: Interdisciplinary
report.Desc: This class builds upon the concepts learned in IDIS 190 with the John M. Perkins Leadership Fellows. The students will deepen their understanding of institutional, cultural and internalized racism, the church's role and the way it persists today. Further, students will explore ways to dismantle institutional racism in working toward the Beloved Community and Shalom. They will also be invited to engage in the redemptive practice of caucusing to address misshapen internalized racial identities.
report.Notes: This section is reserved for Perkins Fellows.

Students consider implications of social research findings for practice and policy. Through the course, students develop an awareness of the importance of social science research as a means to understand ourselves and the world around us.

Students learn how neural networks compute and are trained, how to train them, and how to apply them to tasks such as image classification. The course emphasizes hands-on implementation, evaluation of system performance, and discernment of philosophical, societal, historical, and religious aspects of AI systems. Lab fee.

Students examine computational architectures, learn practical techniques for building and evaluating ML-powered applications, and discern the trajectory and implications of the machine learning approach to AI. As a continuation of CS 375, the course emphasizes hands-on implementation, evaluation of system performance, and discernment of philosophical, societal, historical, and religious aspects of AI systems. Lab fee.

This course will emphasize both principles and practices. Lab fee.

Students will examine possible ways in which they can make contributions to the field of ceramics and visual culture.

Critical theory specific to ceramics is addressed through readings, lectures, and class projects.

report.Subject: Music

The course will consider how Western musical patterns relating to time, pitch, and structure are similar to and different from musical patterns in the non-West. It will also provide an opportunity to reflect on how and why humans create patterns out of sound and why God created us to be musical.

report.Subject: Music
report.Desc: This is an introductory course in historically-informed critical and perceptive listening to music. The relationship between musical style and culture is examined as is the forming of style by the manner in which the ingredients and elements of music are employed. Western art music is emphasized but also included are contemporary popular music and either pre-modern music or non- Western music. No previous musical training is required.

report.Subject: Music

In addition to preparation for weekly lessons, students will be expected to participate in studio classes with fellow composition students, write scores for their compositions using music notation software, and organize performances or recordings of their work for evaluation. Fee - see catalog for details.

report.Desc: This is a study of select musical cultures of Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Europe, and the Americas, with a focus on their various musical styles (traditional and contemporary) and the roles of music in these cultures. No previous musical training is required.

Students will gain knowledge of music curricula, pedagogy, classroom instruments, and classroom technology for teaching. Students will develop an educational philosophy for teaching general music, as well as skills and professionalism necessary for effective instruction. All of these areas are examined through the lens of a Reformed Christian perspective.

report.Subject: Kinesiology
report.Locations: Van Noord Arena 110 - Fitness Classroom; Online - Asynchronous
report.Desc: This class and lab-based course will introduce students to the methods and skills necessary for muscular strength and flexibility (MSF) assessment and prescription for healthy adults, as well as the principles of strength training group leadership and individualized personal training. Topics include muscular strength, endurance, power, and flexibility assessment, 2) the benefits and risks associated with resistance training, 3) selection and prescription of appropriate resistance and flexibility training modalities based on fitness assessment, 4) common orthopedic considerations, and 5) ability to safely demonstrate and lead exercises. Students will learn to conduct a comprehensive workout to include evaluation, warm-up, training bout, cool-down, and flexibility modalities.

report.Subject: Biochemistry
report.Desc: How does chemistry help us understand biological systems? This course is an introduction to the principles of biochemistry in which we focus on the structure and function of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids. The fundamentals of signaling and metabolism and their associated mechanisms of regulation will also be introduced.

report.Subject: Art History
report.Desc: ARTH 133 introduces some of the most notable paintings, prints, and decorative arts produced in Europe from 1700 to 1900. The rise of new public audiences for art, alongside traditional court structures, is a central concern. Gender and the status of women artists are also important themes.

report.Subject: Art History
report.Desc: How do visual conventions developed during the last five hundred years inform what is possible to communicate with an image today? As part of the curriculum of the graphic design major, this course provides a foundation for engaging contemporary visual design in relation to the past five centuries of artistic production. The course attends particularly to the history of printmaking, typography, and compositional conventions, paying special attention to the emergence of consumer cultures and public engagements with print culture, from seventeenth-century broadsides to twentieth-century mass media).

report.Section_Title: Introduction to Social Work and Social Welfare
report.Subject: Social Work
report.Desc: Students will discover what it means to be a professional social worker in this course. With attention to the importance of diversity, history, and the experiences of at-risk populations, students will explore the range of social services and advocacy opportunities for work with individuals, families, groups, communities, and organizations. This will include an exploration of several areas of practice, such as poverty and inequality, housing and homelessness, family and child welfare, health and health care, disability, mental health, substance use, and criminal justice. Students will approach social issues from a strengths-based and systems-based view of persons in their environment.

report.Section_Title: Tropical Ecosystems: Conservation and Development in Belize
report.Subject: Biology
report.Desc: Tropical ecosystems contain the highest concentration of Earth’s biodiversity. Under the pressures of human population growth and resource use, they are also experiencing the highest rates of biodiversity loss. How can successful conservation work occur such that the well-being of local people is not compromised or even promoted? How can human-centered development work be done in such a way that the natural ecosystem to which humans belong is not degraded? These fundamental questions will be engaged through daily field trips to a variety of tropical habitats in Belize—including coral reefs, mangrove swamps, rivers and streams, tropical rain forests, and mountain pinelands. Course participants will be hosted by local Belizean institutions, scientists, and private citizens involved in conservation and sustainability efforts. Course evaluation: daily journal, active participation in course activities and evening discussions, one written test. In preparation, students will attend three two-hour sessions during the fall semester and complete some assigned readings.

The balance of the course examines the changes and continuities that have characterized the post-war period: economic integration, the Cold War and its aftermath, immigration, decolonization, the tension between European unity and national identities, as well as the burden of Europe's past.

report.Subject: Chemistry
report.Desc: Features a problem-solving approach that incorporates sampling, sample preparation, separation of analytes from interfering substances, measurement and data analysis interpretation. Quantitative analysis is presented in the context of analytical methods that include statistics of sample measurements (significance tests, outlier tests, linear regression), separation science (gas, liquid, and chromatography), optical spectroscopy (UV-visible, fluorescence, and atomic absorption spectroscopy), and electrochemistry (electrode potentials, and ion-selective electrodes). Highly recommended for 1st and 2nd year students, and not open to seniors except by permission.
